title: Buddhist caves in India: Ajanta, Ellora, Karla, Bhaja and Kanheri
seo_title: Buddhist Caves in India: Ajanta, Ellora, Karla and Kanheri
meta_description: Buddhist caves in India explained: chaityas and viharas at Ajanta, Ellora, Karla, Bhaja and Kanheri, how they were cut, who paid for them and what to see.
summary: India's Buddhist caves are monasteries and prayer halls cut into rock, mostly in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, from about the 2nd century BCE to the 7th century CE. The main types are the chaitya (a hall with a stupa) and the vihara (a residence for monks). Ajanta, Ellora, Karla, Bhaja and Kanheri are the best known.

sections.h2: Why Buddhist monks cut caves into rock
paras: Buddhist monks spent the monsoon months in one place, and monasteries grew up to house them. In the Western Ghats, the hard basalt cliffs offered a durable alternative to timber and brick: halls cut into rock would last for centuries. Many cave sites sit near ancient trade routes linking ports on the Konkan coast with the Deccan plateau, and inscriptions show merchants, guilds, craftsmen, monks, nuns and rulers paying for caves, pillars and cisterns.

There are well over a thousand rock-cut caves in Maharashtra alone, and most of the earliest are Buddhist. They are a major chapter in Indian architecture, which our lecture on [rock-cut sacred architecture](rock-cut-sacred-architecture.html) covers alongside Hindu and Jain examples.

sections.h2: Chaitya and vihara: the two main cave types
paras: A chaitya (also chaityagriha) is a prayer hall. The classic form is long and apsidal, with a rounded end, rows of pillars separating a central nave from side aisles, and a rock-cut stupa at the far end that worshippers could walk around. The ceiling is often carved to imitate wooden ribs, and a large horseshoe-shaped window above the entrance lets in light.

A vihara is a monastery: a central hall with small cells cut into the walls where monks lived and slept, often with stone benches. In later viharas, especially at Ajanta, a shrine with an image of the Buddha was added at the back wall, reflecting changes in Buddhist practice.

sections.h2: The early caves: Bhaja, Karla and Kanheri
paras: Bhaja, near Lonavala, is among the earliest of the Western Indian caves, usually dated to around the 2nd century BCE. Its chaitya shows clearly how the cave cutters copied timber architecture, and wooden beams were once fitted into the rock. A group of stupas cut in the rock and some early relief sculpture add to its interest.

Karla, not far from Bhaja, has one of the largest and finest early chaitya halls in India, generally dated to around the 1st century CE. Its pillars are topped with sculpted pairs of elephants and riders, and its entrance has carved donor couples. Inscriptions record gifts from donors including merchants.

Kanheri, inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park in Mumbai, is a large complex with more than a hundred caves cut over several centuries, along with water cisterns, rock-cut steps and a big chaitya. It shows how a monastic settlement functioned over a long period. Our guided visit to the [Kanheri caves](kanheri-caves-monastic-landscapes.html) follows the water systems as well as the halls.

sections.h2: Ajanta caves: two phases and famous paintings
paras: Ajanta, in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) district, has about 30 caves cut into a horseshoe-shaped bend of the Waghora river. They were made in two broad phases: an early group from around the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, and a later group mostly from the 5th century CE, under the Vakataka dynasty.

Ajanta is world-famous for its wall paintings, which illustrate the Jataka tales (stories of the Buddha's previous lives) and scenes from his life, with courtly figures, animals and architecture. They are among the most important surviving examples of early Indian painting. Ajanta was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

sections.h2: Ellora: Buddhist caves among Hindu and Jain ones
paras: Ellora, also near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, has about 34 major caves cut from roughly the 6th to the 10th century CE. Caves 1 to 12 are Buddhist, caves 13 to 29 are Hindu, including the Kailasa temple, and caves 30 to 34 are Jain. Ellora became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, together with Ajanta.

The Buddhist caves at Ellora include Cave 10, a chaitya sometimes called Vishvakarma, with a seated Buddha in front of the stupa, and multi-storey viharas such as Caves 11 and 12, which show later Buddhist monastic planning on a large scale.

sections.h2: Not every cave is Buddhist: Udayagiri-Khandagiri and Elephanta
paras: Visitors sometimes assume that every early cave complex is Buddhist. The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar are Jain, cut for Jain monks around the 1st century BCE; the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela is there. A visit to [Udayagiri-Khandagiri](udayagiri-khandagiri-caves-jain-heritage.html) makes a useful comparison with the Buddhist caves of the west.

Elephanta, in Mumbai harbour, is a Hindu cave temple dedicated to Shiva, famous for its great three-headed image, and the Udayagiri caves near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh are Gupta-period Hindu caves. Our wider guide to [famous archaeological sites in India](famous-archaeological-sites-in-india.html) places these sites in a timeline.

faq.q: Which are the oldest Buddhist caves in India?
faq.a: Among the oldest rock-cut caves in India are the Barabar caves in Bihar, cut under the Mauryas for the Ajivika sect rather than Buddhists. Among Buddhist caves, Bhaja, Pitalkhora, Kondane and the early caves at Ajanta are usually dated to around the 2nd century BCE.

faq.q: What is the difference between a chaitya and a vihara?
faq.a: A chaitya is a prayer hall, usually long with a rounded end and a stupa that worshippers walked around. A vihara is a monastery: a hall surrounded by small cells where monks lived. Large cave sites usually have both, along with cisterns for water.

Ellora has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves. Caves 1 to 12 are Buddhist, caves 13 to 29 are Hindu, including the Kailasa temple, and caves 30 to 34 are Jain. The site shows these traditions existing side by side between about the 6th and 10th centuries CE.

faq.q: Are Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves Buddhist?
faq.a: No. The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar in Odisha are Jain. They were cut as residences for Jain monks, mostly around the 1st century BCE, and include the Hathigumpha inscription of King Kharavela, a supporter of Jainism.

faq.q: Which Buddhist caves can I visit from Mumbai or Pune?
faq.a: Kanheri is inside Mumbai, in Sanjay Gandhi National Park. Karla and Bhaja lie near Lonavala, between Mumbai and Pune, and Bedse is nearby. Ajanta and Ellora are best reached from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Check the ASI website for current visiting arrangements before you go.

bundle.title: Mumbai's two cave traditions
bundle.pitch: Kanheri's Buddhist monastery and Elephanta's Shiva temple, seen with a lecture on rock-cut architecture, show how different communities shaped rock.

audience_hooks: Schools: a guided visit to Kanheri caves in Mumbai with an archaeologist.
Colleges: a lecture on rock-cut sacred architecture, online or on campus.
Travellers: a private multi-day journey through Mumbai's caves and living traditions.

descriptions: Guided visits to Kanheri and Elephanta, with lectures on rock-cut architecture.
Day visits and journeys through India's cave sites for schools and private groups.

posts.hook: The ribbed ceilings at Bhaja copy wooden roofs.
posts.caption: Early cave cutters imitated timber buildings in stone, down to the rafters. Some caves even had real wooden beams fixed into the rock.

posts.hook: In a chaitya hall, walk around the stupa.
posts.caption: The pillared aisles were made for circumambulation. Walk the path the monks walked and the plan of the hall makes sense.

posts.hook: A Buddhist monastery inside Mumbai city limits.
posts.caption: Kanheri has over a hundred caves, cisterns and stairways. We lead guided visits for schools and groups, with an optional lecture on rock-cut architecture beforehand.

social.reel: Walk-through shot entering the Karla chaitya, camera rising to the ribbed ceiling, then down to the stupa. On-screen line: 'Cut from one rock, about 2,000 years ago.' End card: 'Buddhist caves with an archaeologist.'
